summary: Presents an object-oriented information model of IPsec policy, to help people agree on what policy means. Task-specific forms, such as storage schemas and distribution formats, can be derived from it. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Security rules for a network have lots of parts. This memo draws a careful plan of the parts and how they relate, so different tools can share the same understanding.

questions: what is the ipsec policy information model
what is the difference between ikerule and ipsecrule
how do ipsec policy rules execute actions
subtitle: A shared object-oriented blueprint for describing IPsec rules, so storage formats and tools can all mean the same thing.

tldr.problem: IPsec policy gets stored in directories, sent over policy protocols, written in text languages and edited as XML. Without one canonical description, each form can drift in what the policy actually means.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3585 defines an object-oriented information model, drawn as UML classes, that extends the Policy Core Information Model. It describes IPsec and IKE rules, conditions, actions, proposals, transforms, peers and identities.
tldr.outcome: Task-specific forms such as storage schemas, distribution formats and policy languages can be derived from this one model. It is a Proposed Standard and the text does not say that anything replaced it.

today: RFC 3585 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for it lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this IPsec policy information model, which builds on the PCIM of RFC 3060 and the extensions of RFC 3460.

sections.title: Why a Policy Model
sections.content:
IPsec policy takes many forms as it travels from storage, to distribution, to the places where decisions are made. The RFC lists examples: a schema in an LDAP directory, an on-the-wire representation over a protocol such as COPS, a text-based policy language an administrator can edit, or an XML document.

Each of these task-specific representations should be derived from a canonical one that precisely states the content and meaning of the policy. This document supplies that task-independent form. It focuses on the existing protocols (IPComp, ESP, AH, the IPsec DOI and IKE), and because the model is object-oriented it can be extended.

The model is drawn as a UML static class diagram. It is a conceptual view meant to aid understanding, not a class-for-class recipe: an LDAP implementation, for example, may flatten it into fewer classes because following references is inefficient.
sections.eli5: Imagine every group building a house from its own sketch. This memo is the one master blueprint, so everyone builds the same house.

sections.title: Building on PCIM and the Class Hierarchy
sections.content:
The IPsec model derives from the classes in the Policy Core Information Model (PCIM, RFC 3060) and its extensions (PCIMe, RFC 3460), which in turn come from the DMTF Common Information Model (CIM). The RFC gives two inheritance trees: one for ordinary classes and one for association classes that link them.

A PolicyGroup holds the policies used on an interface. It SHOULD be tied either directly to the IPProtocolEndpoint that represents the interface, through IPsecPolicyForEndpoint, or indirectly to the hosting System, through IPsecPolicyForSystem. When an endpoint has no group of its own, the system's group is used.

Inside a group sit rules. SARule is the base class, with IKERule for IKE phase 1 and IPsecRule for IKE phase 2 for the IPsec DOI. SARule is concrete in form but MUST NOT be instantiated, and each SARule in a valid PolicyGroup MUST have a unique priority number.

The IKE and IPsec rules are used to build or negotiate the IPsec Security Association Database (SADB). The IPsec rules represent the Security Policy Database. The SADB itself is not modeled.
sections.eli5: Rules live in folders, and each folder belongs to a network connection or to the whole computer. If a connection has no folder, it uses the computer's folder.

sections.title: How Rules Are Applied
sections.content:
The RFC walks through four cases. An outgoing unprotected packet is checked against the IPsec rules. On a match the SADB is checked, and if there is no matching SA and the rule requires IKE, the IKE rules are used. The negotiated or preconfigured SA is then installed in the SADB. An incoming protected packet is also checked against the IPsec rules, and a preconfigured SA may be installed if none exists. An incoming IKE packet that is not part of an existing IKE SA is checked against the IKE rules.

Each rule holds a list of ordered actions and an ExecutionStrategy that decides how they run. Do Until Success tries actions in ActionOrder until one works, which gives fallbacks such as main mode then aggressive mode, or an IPsec transport action then a bypass. Do All runs every action regardless of failures, which suits nested SAs. Do Until Failure is inherited from PCIMe and is not expected to be useful for IPsec. For rules, Mandatory MUST be true if present, SequencedActions MUST be mandatory if present, and PolicyDecisionStrategy must be FirstMatching if present.

The LimitNegotiation property restricts the role a rule may play: 1 for initiator-only, 2 for responder-only, 3 for both. It applies to new negotiations, not to refreshing an existing SA. A rule can also carry IdentityContexts, strings such as a VPN name, combined with OR across array values and AND with && inside one value.
sections.eli5: When a packet shows up, the computer goes down its list of rules until one fits. A rule can say try this, and if that fails try that, or do all of these steps in order.

sections.title: Conditions and Filters
sections.content:
The condition classes build the if part of a rule. SACondition is the anchor: it ties a rule to one filter list through FilterOfSACondition, and to trusted credential sources through AcceptCredentialsFrom. A rule MUST contain at least one SACondition. Condition parts that have nothing to evaluate count as true, unless the protocol finished without providing the required information.

Four kinds of filter entry are used. IPHeadersFilter comes from PCIMe and matches 5-tuples, and for symmetric matching the filter list's Direction SHOULD be Mirrored. CredentialFilterEntry matches parts of a credential, such as X.509 certificate attributes like subjectName, or Kerberos tickets, and a wildcard character may appear in the match value. IPSOFilterEntry matches the IP Security Options of RFC 1108, for example a classification level of 61 for TopSecret or 90 for Secret. PeerIDPayloadFilterEntry matches the ID payload in an IKE exchange, for example *@example.com or 193.190.125.0/24.

The peer ID filter applies only to IKE rules acting as responder. It can be used at once in aggressive mode, but its use is delayed in main mode. If a credential filter fails during IKE, the negotiation MUST stop and the triggering IKE action fails.
sections.eli5: A condition is like a bouncer's checklist: where is this coming from, what ID badge does it show, and how secret is it. If the checklist matches, the rule applies.

sections.title: Actions
sections.content:
Actions say what a device does when a condition matches. The abstract base is SAAction, which carries logging flags: DoActionLogging and DoPacketLogging. It splits into two branches.

Static actions need no negotiation. IPsecBypassAction lets packets flow in the clear. IPsecDiscardAction drops them. IKERejectAction refuses to attempt IKE with a peer, which helps resist some denial of service attacks when acting as responder. PreconfiguredSAAction creates an SA from hard-wired algorithms and keys, in transport or tunnel form, and the SPI comes from the TransformOfPreconfiguredAction association. A static action has a LifetimeSeconds, where zero means an infinite lifetime.

Negotiation actions go through IKE. IKEAction sets phase 1 parameters, including ExchangeMode (1 base, 2 main, 4 aggressive). IPsecTransportAction and IPsecTunnelAction set phase 2 parameters, including UsePFS for perfect forward secrecy, a GroupId for the key exchange group and a Granularity that shapes the selector. Tunnel actions also choose DFHandling for the Don't Fragment bit, and use an ordered list of PeerGateway objects. Minimum lifetime properties exist to stop a peer forcing costly renegotiations with an arbitrarily low lifetime.
sections.eli5: An action is what the computer does once a rule fits: let the packet through, throw it away, or lock it in a secret code first. Some secret codes are agreed with the other side, and some are set up in advance.

sections.title: Proposals and Transforms
sections.content:
A negotiation action points to an ordered list of SAProposal objects through ContainedProposal, and a lower SequenceNumber means a more preferred proposal. An IKEProposal names the phase 1 cipher, hash, optional pseudo-random function, key exchange group, authentication method and maximum lifetimes. Setting the seconds lifetime to zero means the default of 8 hours.

An IPsecProposal is made of SATransform objects through ContainedTransform. The transforms are AHTransform, ESPTransform and IPCOMPTransform. Transforms of the same type are logically ORed in preference order, while transforms of different types are ANDed. In the RFC's example, an ESP list of two choices and an AH list of two choices means the receiver should pick one from each list.

ESP and AH transforms can switch replay prevention on and set a sliding window size in bits, and the window is assumed to be a power of 2. ESP transforms add a cipher key length in bits. IPComp transforms identify a compression algorithm, with a vendor-specific option.
sections.eli5: A proposal is a menu of offers, like saying I can do pizza or pasta, pizza is better. The other side picks something from the menu that works for both.

sections.title: IKE Service, Peers and Identities
sections.content:
The last group of classes holds extra information needed to apply policy. IKEService represents the IKE negotiation function of a system. There may be several on one system, but only one per interface. It uses tables of peers and a set of settings for SAs that start automatically.

A PeerGateway names a security gateway to negotiate with by name, identity type and identity value. A PeerIdentityTable collects PeerIdentityEntry objects that map a peer's identity to its address, and an entry's address type is 0 for unknown, 1 for IPv4 or 2 for IPv6. A pre-shared key for a peer is kept in a CIM SharedSecret object rather than in the entry.

AutostartIKESetting lets a service start negotiations, or install static SAs, when it is initialized. Settings are grouped into an AutostartIKEConfiguration, and a SequenceNumber of zero means order does not matter. IKEIdentity represents the identities that the local IKE service can present on an endpoint or a collection of endpoints. Together with the identity type from the IKE action and the rule's contexts, it selects one identity, and there SHOULD be exactly one.
sections.eli5: This part is the address book and the name tags. It lists who the other computers are, what name tag each wears, and which of your own name tags to show them.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements and Security
sections.content:
Section 9 of the RFC is a long table that marks every class, property, association and reference as MUST, SHOULD or MAY. Core pieces such as SARule, IKERule, IPsecRule, SACondition, the proposals and the IKE and IPsec actions are marked MUST. Many extras are MAY, including the IKEService and identity classes, IPCOMPTransform, IPSOFilterEntry and CredentialFilterEntry.

For security, the document states that it only describes an information model and does not detail security requirements for storage or delivery. Physical models derived from it MUST implement the relevant security. Most classes (the RFC names IpHeadersFilter and SAAction) MUST at least provide the integrity service, and other data, such as a SharedSecret in PeerIdentityEntry or PreconfiguredSAAction, MUST also receive the confidentiality service.
sections.eli5: The memo lists which parts every builder must include and which are optional. It also says that whoever stores these rules must keep them from being changed, and keep secret keys secret.

items.label: subnet
items.desc: The source and destination subnet masks of the filter entry are used.

items.label: address
items.desc: Only the source and destination IP addresses of the triggering packet are used.

items.label: protocol
items.desc: Source and destination addresses plus the IP protocol of the triggering packet are used.

items.label: port
items.desc: Addresses, IP protocol and the source and destination layer 4 ports are used.
